content: To calculate the proportion of leprosy cases detected among household contacts, the total number of cases detected in a specific area (global, national, state, province, district) is divided by the total number of registered household contacts in that area. This value is then multiplied by 100 to express it as a percentage. This proportion serves as an indicator of the coverage of case detection among household contacts of registered patients in a given area, such as a village, urban area, or health center. A higher percentage is considered better, as household contacts represent the highest-risk group for contracting leprosy in any country. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020: Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world was officially launched on April 20, 2016. Its primary goal is to further reduce the burden of leprosy while ensuring comprehensive and timely care, guided by principles of equity and social justice. The strategy emphasizes three main pillars: strengthening government ownership and partnerships, stopping leprosy and its complications, and eliminating discrimination while promoting inclusion. The strategy provides a framework for national leprosy program managers to adapt and implement these actions in their respective countries, aiming to achieve the global targets set for 2020. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed an operational manual to guide the implementation of the Global Leprosy Strategy. This manual includes suggested actions under each of the three strategic pillars and is designed to be adapted to national contexts. It was created with input from various stakeholders, including national program managers, technical agencies, funding agencies, and nongovernmental organizations. The WHO has also published several guidelines and reports to support leprosy control efforts, including enhanced global strategies for reducing the disease burden (2011–2015), guidelines for drug resistance surveillance, and recommendations for strengthening the participation of individuals affected by leprosy in service delivery. Additionally, WHO has provided resources for self-care to prevent disabilities, training materials for healthcare workers, and technical guides for integrating leprosy services into broader health systems. Leprosy-related stigma and discrimination remain significant challenges. Studies have systematically reviewed the social stigma associated with neglected tropical diseases, including leprosy, and have proposed interventions to reduce stigma and improve the quality of life for affected individuals. Research has also explored the use of chemoprophylaxis and immunoprophylaxis to protect individuals at risk of leprosy, as well as the potential of single-dose rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis without inducing resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The WHO and other organizations have emphasized the importance of addressing the social and psychological impacts of leprosy, including stigma and discrimination. Efforts to eliminate discrimination against individuals affected by leprosy and their families have been supported by the United Nations Human Rights Council, which has issued resolutions and guidelines to promote inclusion and protect human rights. The operational manual and related resources aim to provide practical tools for achieving the goals of the Global Leprosy Strategy, ensuring that countries can effectively address the medical, social, and psychological aspects of leprosy while working towards its elimination.
